docs.title: Ensembl VEP
docs.text:
Ensembl VEP (Variant Effect Predictor) predicts the functional effects of genomic variants.

NOTE: This project is in an initial development phase. Many features are incomplete, APIs may change without notice, and documentation is partial. Use at your own risk and feel free to open issues or contribute; your feedback is welcome.

docs.title: Typing Conventions
docs.text:
All code must use explicit type annotations for function signatures, class attributes, and variables where appropriate.

Rules: - Use standard Python typing (PEP 484, PEP 604). - For return types that may be a value or None, use Type | None instead of Optional[Type]. This is more cleaner. Also type checking does not happen at runtime, so does not affect users using python < 3.10 unless we are using type introspection dynamically at runtime.

  • Example: 
    def get_feature() -> Feature | None:
    ...
    Instead of: 
    def get_feature() -> Optional[Feature]:
    ...
  • Use built-in types where possible (e.g., list, dict, str).
  • Always annotate arguments and return values in public class, functions etc. Exceptions can be tests and private functions.

We will enforce these conventions through static analysis tools (e.g., mypy) as part of our CI pipeline to ensure consistency and catch type-related issues early in the development process.

docs.title: Logging Implementation
docs.text:
All logging in this project should use Python's built-in logging module. The recommended setup is as follows:

  • logging.basicConfig has been used in ensembl.vep.common.setup_logging function to setup logging configuration. This function should be called at the entry point of the application to ensure consistent logging behavior across all modules.
  • Log messages is sent to a file named {output_file}_warnings.txt consistent with old Ensembl VEP.
  • The log format includes timestamp, log level, logger name, and message.
  • For timestamps (%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S) ISO 8601 format is used.
  • Always use named loggers (logging.getLogger(__name__)) for module-level logging.

Example setup in a module:

import logging

logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)

def some_function():
    logger.info("This is an info message.")
    logger.warning("This is a warning message.")

Open question: Should we have a backward compatible option to have same manner of message formatting as old VEP?

docs.title: Docstring Style
docs.text:
All docstrings in this project must follow the Google Python Style Guide for docstrings.

Rationale: - Google style docstrings provide clear, consistent documentation and improve readability. - The docstring will facilitate automated documentation generation using mkdocs.

No docstring, no visibility in the public docs!

Key points: - Use triple double quotes (""") for all docstrings. - Include sections for Args, Returns, Raises, and Examples as appropriate. - Document types for all parameters and return values. - Keep descriptions concise and informative.

docs.title: Class Naming
docs.text:
Class names must use CapWords (e.g., MyClass), in line with widely accepted Python conventions and PEP 8 guidelines.

We are deliberately not using the Base prefix. Classes are named to reflect the object they model, and extended (if need be) via inheritance using progressively specific names using meaningful prefixes rather than just Base — for example, Variation as the parent class and StructuralVariation as its subclass.

Rationale: This is a matter of stylistic preference — both approaches offer the same extensibility.

docs.title: Non-derived attributes
docs.text: Attributes that are not derived from other attributes are defined in the class body with type annotations. They are generally not lazy-loaded or cached and further categorised into core attributes and externally-set attributes.

docs.title: Core Attributes
docs.text:
Core attributes are those that are set during object initialization and are essential to the object's identity. They are included in the __init__ method generated by attrs. They do not have default values.

from ensembl.vep.common import UnsafeSetterMixin, invalidates
class MyClass(UnsafeSetterMixin):
    core_attr1: int = field(on_setattr=invalidates('derived_attr1'))
    core_attr2: str
    derived_attr1: int = field(init=False)

    def some_method(self):
        derived_attr1 = self.core_attr1 * 2

cls = MyClass(core_attr1=1, core_attr2="foo")
with cls.unsafe():
    cls.core_attr1 = 2

docs.title: Externally-set attributes
docs.text:
These are similarly not derived and externally set like core attributes but they are not essential to be in the __init__ method. The class is not responsible for calculating these attributes, so it should not enforce immutability or caching.

They should still be defined in the class body (with type annotations) to be compatible with slots=True and to ensure they are tracked properly.

class MyClass():
    core_attr: int
    externally_set_attr: int = field(init=False)

cls = MyClass(core_attr=1)
cls.externally_set_attr = some_external_method()

docs.title: Derived Attributes
docs.text:
Derived attributes are read-only properties derived from one or more attributes. They are lazy-loaded (not part of __init__) and can be cached (using functools.cached_property).

Read-only enforcement is handled by the using a combination of a protected variable (prefixing name with _) and a public variable property with no setter. The public variable should be used for all access outside of the class definition, the protected variable is for internal use only. Because the public accessible variable has no setter, you should never assign directly to it, mypy will throw a misc error if you do (property is read-only). Reading or assigning to the protected variable directly outside of the class definition will result in a W202 error by pylint. Both will fail the CI checks and should be avoided. Ensure mypy and pylint are enabled in your IDE for linting annotations during development.

Seeding a derived attribute at (or after) construction: sometimes a derived attribute genuinely needs an escape hatch -- the common case is normally computed, but a caller occasionally has an authoritative value and wants to supply it directly instead of it being derived. Do not make the derived property itself directly writable to solve this (see the note at the end of this subsection for why). Two options, in order of preference:

  • Feature.derived_attr_seeds (a constructor-only kwarg every Feature subclass inherits): pass {"attr_name": value} and it pre-populates that attribute's protected slot before anything else runs, so the property returns the seeded value instead of computing one -- indistinguishable from a normally-computed value from that point on, including being cleared by whatever invalidates() hooks would clear a computed one. 
    transcript = Transcript(..., derived_attr_seeds={"cds": my_authoritative_cds})
assert transcript.cds is my_authoritative_cds  # never ran the normal CDS derivation
  • Feature.seed_attrs(**seeds): the same mechanism, callable at any time rather than only at construction. Needed whenever the attribute you want to seed depends on another field that is itself init=False (so it can only be assigned after construction, e.g. Transcript.spliced_exons) -- seeding at construction time would just be invalidated the moment that field is assigned afterwards. 
    transcript.spliced_exons = [...]  # init=False -- must be set post-construction
transcript.seed_attrs(cds=my_authoritative_cds)  # now safe: nothing left to invalidate it

For a one-off bespoke _override field instead of this generic mechanism (still a valid, slightly more explicit alternative -- see Translation.exon_coding_end_override), see the pattern below for how to keep the override and the normal derivation composed safely, and note the more advanced case: if a derived attribute needs to check whether a different derived attribute was itself already seeded or computed (not just its own core-attribute inputs), reading that sibling through its normal public property is unsafe if the two can derive from each other -- ordinary attribute access (including getattr(obj, name, default)) still triggers computation on a miss, default or not. Use ensembl.vep.common.is_resolved(instance, "_sibling_name") instead: it checks whether the protected slot already has a value without ever computing one, by calling the slot descriptor's own __get__ directly rather than going through the class's normal (compute-on-miss) attribute lookup. See Transcript._locate_coding_boundary (models/genic/transcript.py) for a real case where this matters: exon_coding_start can derive from a seeded cds, and cds can derive from exon_coding_start -- is_resolved is what lets each direction check "did the other side already get an answer from somewhere else" without ever triggering the recursive case.

Lazy-loading is achieved by setting init=False for the derived attribute, which means it will not be included in the __init__ method and will only be computed when accessed.

Caching is implemented using functools.cached_property on the private variable, which stores the computed value after the first access and returns the cached value on subsequent accesses. In some cases, the derived attribute may not be cached, - if the computation is cheap and does not justify the overhead of caching, or - if the derived attribute is set by product of some internal computation and does not have its own function to be decorated with @cached_property.

class MyClass(CachedAttributeGuardMixin):
    core_attr1: int
    _derived_attr3: int = field(init=False, default=0)    # default value for non-cached derived attribute that is set by internal computation

    @property
    def derived_attr1(self) -> int:
        return self._derived_attr1

    @cached_property
    def _derived_attr1(self) -> int:
        # perform expensive computation here using core_attr1
        return sum(range(self.core_attr1 * 2))

    @property
    def derived_attr2(self) -> int:
        # perform cheap computation here using core_attr1
        # does not justify caching
        return self.core_attr1 + 1

    @property
    def derived_attr3(self) -> int:
        # this attribute is set by some internal computation
        return self._derived_attr3

    @cached_property
    def _derived_attr3(self) -> int:
        # alternative to defining default value at attribute definition
        # can be used for some minor compuations for initial value assignment
        return 0

    def some_internal_computation(self):
        # perform some internal computation here and set derived_attr3
        # cannot do caching
        self._derived_attr3 = self.core_attr1 * 2

docs.title: Cache invalidation
docs.text:
It is expected that core attributes are not changed after initialization. In the unlikely event they do need to be updated, the related derived attributes needs to be invalidated. Some derived attribute may also depend on other derived attributes, we may need to invalidate those as well.

INVALIDATING USING A ATTRIBUTE WHOSE init=False is PROBLAMETIC; as it is not part of constructor when it is assigned and between object creation we might have some seeded value for the derived attribute.

Invalidating cache dependent on core attributes: This is handled by using the invalidates hook with on_setattr. This has speed penalty for object creation and assignment of core attributes. Core attributes are not expected to be updated that much. 

class MyClass:
    core_attr1: int = field(on_setattr=invalidates('_derived_attr1'))

    @property
    def derived_attr1(self) -> int:
        return self._derived_attr1

    @cached_property
    def _derived_attr1(self) -> int:
        # perform expensive computation here using core_attr1
        return sum(range(self.core_attr1 * 2))

Invalidating cache dependent on derived attributes: Derived attributes may not be defined in the attribute list, so we cannot use invalidates hook. Instead, we can directly call invalidate function from the function that calculates the derived attribute that the other derived attribute depends on.

class MyClass():
    core_attr1: int

    @property
    def derived_attr1(self) -> int:
        return self._derived_attr1

    @cached_property
    def _derived_attr1(self) -> int:
        invalidate(self, '_derived_attr2')  # invalidate dependent derived attribute

        # perform expensive computation here using core_attr1
        return sum(range(self.core_attr1 * 2))

    @property
    def derived_attr2(self) -> int:
        return self._derived_attr2

    @cached_property
    def _derived_attr2(self) -> int:
        # perform expensive computation here using derived_attr1
        return self.derived_attr1 + 1

Resetting derived attribute which does not have its own function: In some cases, the derived attribute is set by some internal computation and does not have its own function to be decorated with @cached_property (third case mentioned in Derived Attributes). So, if we invalidate the attribute and in some place we try to access it, we will run into error. In such cases, we can use reset_attrs that will instead of invalidating the attribute, reset it to its default state.

Note: In some cases, we may want to allow updating core attributes without invalidating derived attributes. In that case, we can also use the UnsafeSetterMixin mixin. It allows using context managers to temporarily disable cache invalidation for faster but unsafe attribute update. Generally this should not be necessary. ```python class MyClass(UnsafeSetterMixin): core_attr1: int = field(on_setattr=invalidates('_derived_attr1'))

@property
def derived_attr1(self) -> int:
    return self._derived_attr1

@cached_property
def _derived_attr1(self) -> int:
    # perform expensive computation here using core_attr1
    return sum(range(self.core_attr1 * 2))

cls = MyClass(core_attr1=1) with cls.unsafe(): cls.core_attr1 = 2 # does not invalidate derived_attr1 

### Use of attrs

We heavily use the `attrs` module for writing classes. All classes use the following `attrs` decorator defaults:

**`slots = True`**

Slotted classes are enabled by default for improved memory efficiency and attribute access performance.

**Caveat:** Slotted classes come with known limitations. Refer to the [attrs glossary on slotted classes](https://www.attrs.org/en/stable/glossary.html#term-slotted-classes) for a full list.

**Rationale:** This is an intentional design constraint. Requiring all attributes to be declared upfront — including private or cache-related ones — prevents hidden state from accumulating across the codebase. Readers should be able to understand an object's full structure without hunting through unrelated code paths.

**`auto_attribs = True`**

All attributes must have explicit type annotations. This is enforced to maintain consistency and enable static analysis.

**`kw_only = True`**

All constructor arguments are keyword-only. This improves readability at call sites by making argument names self-documenting.

```python
# Good — intent is clear
MyClass(name="foo", value=42)

# Avoided — positional args obscure intent
MyClass("foo", 42)

on_setattr vs Custom __setattr__

We use a custom __setattr__ rather than on_setattr because on_setattr does not trigger for attributes defined via @cached_property — even at the class level. Since we want these cached attributes to be immutable and they cannot be registered in the attrs attribute list, a custom __setattr__ is necessary to enforce that constraint uniformly.

Caveat: This approach may cause performance issues. As setattr is called for every attribute assignment, it can introduce overhead, especially if there are many attributes or frequent updates. This is a trade-off between enforcing immutability and performance.

We can possibly emulate the attrs-generated __setattr__ if required in future - 

def __setattr__(self, name, val):
    try:
        a, hook = sa_attrs[name]
    except KeyError:
        nval = val
    else:
        nval = hook(self, a, val)

    _OBJ_SETATTR(self, name, nval)
This uses a dictionary lookup (sa_attrs) to resolve any validation or conversion hooks, falling back to a plain assignment if the attribute is not registered.

Open questions: - Can __setattr__ be further optimised and eliminate loops and conditionals? - Is there a way to register @cached_property attributes in the attrs attribute list so that they are handled by on_setattr? - Is it better to implement custom caching logic with immutability instead of setattr?

More Open Questions

  • match_args — Should this be explicitly set?
  • collect_by_mro — Should this be explicitly set?

docs.title: Inheritance and Mixins
docs.text:
Since we use slots=True, multiple inheritance is not straightforward — attrs requires that only one of the parent classes can use slots=True. And, if you inherit from class that is not using slots then you lose some of the benefits of slots in the child class especially slot inheritance.

By design, we avoid multiple inheritance and prefer association when shared behaviour is needed.

Rationale: Multiple inheritance is complex and easy to mess up (the infamous deadly diamond of death). You have to be careful with method resolution order (MRO) so that the correct derived methods are called. Then also you have to use super() consistently or never at all.

When shared behaviour cannot be achieved through association, Mixins are the sanctioned exception. A Mixin is a lightweight class that provides a specific set of reusable methods without carrying state. Because they do not use @define or @attrs, they are compatible with slots=True classes and are never meant to be instantiated directly.

Mixins must be defined with empty __slots__ to ensure they do not introduce a __dict__ that would break slot inheritance.

# Correct: Mixin defined with empty slots
class SerialisableMixin:
    __slots__ = ()

    def to_dict(self):
        ...

docs.title: Lazy Loading and Caching
docs.text:
For attributes that are not core attributes, we lazy_load them by setting init=False. Furthermore functools.cached_property is used to cache attributes after first access.

The @cached_property is by default not suitable for use with slotted classes because it relies on the presence of a __dict__ to store cached values. However, as of attrs >= 24.1.0, cached_property is supported on slotted classes. See also: how cached properties work on slotted classes.

Warning: cached_property is not thread-safe by default. If the class may be accessed concurrently, we use a threading lock to guard the property computation. Example: 

from threading import RLock
from attrs import field
from functools import cached_property

class MyClass:
    _lock: RLock = field(factory=RLock, init=False)

    @cached_property
    def expensive_computation(self):
        with self._lock:
            # perform expensive computation here
            ...

Note: The use of RLock instead of Lock to prevent deadlocks when trying to access a cached property from a another cached property.

docs.title: Coordinate Systems and Slices
docs.text:
We use coordinate systems and slices to represent biological sequences, following the conventions established by Ensembl.

A coordinate system defines the reference frame for a biological sequence — for example, a chromosome, clone, or contig. Ensembl uses 1-based indexing, meaning the first base of a sequence is position 1. Coordinate systems themselves carry no concept of strandedness.

A slice represents a defined region within a coordinate system. Slice coordinates are relative to the start of the underlying sequence region, and by convention the start of a slice is always less than or equal to its end, regardless of strandedness. Strandedness is introduced at the slice level — the strand of a slice represents its orientation relative to the default orientation of the sequence region (which should always be forward).

Features positioned on a slice have coordinates and strand values expressed relative to that slice. To obtain a feature's absolute position on the underlying sequence region, the seq_region_start, seq_region_end, and seq_region_strand methods should be used instead.

Note: The concept of a "sequence region" is referenced in various parts of the codebase but has no dedicated class. A slice spanning the full length of a biological sequence with positive strandedness can be considered a functional equivalent of a sequence region.

docs.title: Coordinate Conventions
docs.text:
All positions on a slice or sequence feature use start and end coordinates, where the condition start <= end always holds true.

Exception: 1. Insertion variants described in Ensembl's default format can have end = start - 1. 2. Circular slice on a bacterial or mitochondrial DNA can have end < start.

We use 1-based inclusive (closed) coordinates for all positions. This means that the first base of a sequence is at position 1, and both start and end positions are included in the feature span.

docs.title: Insertion coordinates
docs.text:
As convention in Ensembl, for insertion variants, the start and end coordinates are defined such that end = start - 1. This is because in 1-based inclusive coordinates, length is represented as end - start + 1. An insertion has a length of 0, furthermore the adjacent start and end coordinates clearly indicate the position of the insertion between two bases.

This convention is also convenient for calculating pre and post sequence for shifting algorithm. Nonetheless, it can be a source of confusion and errors, so it is important to be aware of this special case when working with insertion variants.

docs.title: Removal of Reference Bases
docs.text: When Variation objects are created any anchor bases are removed and the coordinates adjusted accordingly. For example, a deletion represented in VCF as 1 10 CAT C becomes AT/- with start=11 and end=12. An insertion such as 1 10 G GAT becomes -/AT with start=11 and end=10. The same is true for symbolic alleles. e.g. This variant 1 100 G <DEL>, becomes -/<DEL> and start is updated to 101.

docs.title: Getting away with circular dependency
docs.text:
The heavy use of subfolders to group similar objects means that, depending on the way we structure our modules, there could be circular dependencies during import. The main source of circular dependencies here comes from using __init__.py files to expose a package's public API.

The circular import is avoided using the following approaches:

docs.title: When importing from same package
docs.text:
When importing within the same package, always import directly from the concrete module rather than through a package's public API.

Prefer: 

from ensembl.vep.models.genic.transcript import Transcript
Over: 
from ensembl.vep.models.genic import Transcript

We also prefer absolute imports over relative imports, even within the same package: Prefer: 

from ensembl.vep.models.genic.transcript import Transcript
Over: 
from .transcript import Transcript
Absolute imports are more explicit, easier to trace, and consistent with PEP 8.

docs.title: Importing for type annotations
docs.text:
When we are importing some module that is solely used for type annotations, typing.TYPE_CHECKING should be used - 

if typing.TYPE_CHECKING:
    from some_module import some_function

It allows importing the module only when type checking is performed (e.g. by static analysis tools), but not during runtime.

docs.title: Prevent direct circular import
docs.text: And, of course, we need to prevent direct circular imports (module A importing module B, and module B importing module A) by making sure we keep one-way dependency direction, i.e. the base class cannot inherit from any of the descendant classes.

docs.title: Containers
docs.text: We are using containers where we do not want to implement any behavior for an object, but useful to have a named and grouped representation of the data. They are defined using @frozen from attrs to create immutable data structures and available in ensembl.vep.common.(containers).

docs.title: How to install this library
docs.text: This Python library requires Python 3.12+ to work.

docs.title: Basic installation
docs.text:
To install it, just run the following command:

pip3 install git+https://github.com/Ensembl/ensembl-vep-py.git

docs.title: Development-oriented installation
docs.text:
To perform a development installation it is advised to use a Python virtual environment (and activate it):

python3 -m venv path/to/virtual_env
source path/to/virtual_env/bin/activate

And then clone the GitHub repository and install it in edit mode:

git clone https://github.com/Ensembl/ensembl-vep-py.git
pip3 install -e ensembl-vep-py/.[cicd,doc]

docs.title: Annotation architecture
docs.text:
This guide describes the annotation path implemented by the default vep run workflow. It is intended for contributors adding a source, match policy, overlap kind, annotation strategy, or execution option.

The design separates retrieval, association, interpretation, and execution. Each layer has one job and can change without making the others understand its storage or algorithm choices.

docs.title: Package responsibilities
docs.text:
Package Responsibility Does not own buffer/ Holds one bounded group of input objects and indexes them for candidate lookup. Source handles or output writing. caches/ Reusable lookup structures, including interval-tree and binned feature caches. Matching policy or consequence logic. matcher/ Pure coordinate and allele association policies. Source fetching, model construction, or caches. overlaps/ Finds candidate pairs and constructs typed overlap models. Consequence interpretation. annotators/ Turns typed overlaps into typed annotation values. Feature retrieval. workflow/ Selects ordered tracks and composes a finder with an annotator. CLI parsing and process management. sources/ Reads source-specific records and builds domain features. Variant-to-feature association policy. runner/ Parses input, creates worker-local runtime state, schedules buffers, preserves output order, and writes output. Domain matching rules. 
flowchart LR
    Runner["runner\nexecution and output"] --> Compiler["workflow compiler\nconfig to plan"]
    Compiler --> Workflow["workflow\nplan and tracks"]
    Workflow --> Finder["overlaps\nfinder"]
    Workflow --> Annotator["annotators\ninterpret overlaps"]
    Runner --> Resolver["source-bound resolver\nmap sequence-region names"]
    Resolver --> Source["sources\nretrieve features"]
    Finder --> Source
    Finder --> Cache["caches\nfeature cache"]
    Finder --> Matcher["matcher\nassociate coordinates or alleles"]
    Finder --> Models["models\ntyped overlaps"]
    Annotator --> Models
    Buffer["buffer\ninput interval index"] --> Finder

workflow is deliberately not named annotation: a workflow is an executable composition of tracks, whereas an annotator is only the part that interprets an overlap.

docs.title: Workflow layout
docs.text:
The workflow package separates reusable track definitions from complete execution plans:

workflow/
├── compiler.py
├── execution.py                 # serial and process execution policy
├── tracks/
│   ├── base.py                    # protocol, values, and overlap implementation
│   ├── registry.py                # track factories only
│   └── transcript_consequence.py  # transcript consequence construction
└── plans/
    ├── base.py                    # workflow specification and runtime plan
    ├── registry.py                # workflow factories only
    ├── default.py                 # default plan construction
    └── haplo.py                   # haplotype plan construction

AnnotationTrack is a protocol. A plan consequently depends on the behaviour it needs rather than a shared superclass. The same tracks/base.py module contains OverlapAnnotationTrack, the standard finder-to-annotator batching implementation. A specialised track remains free to implement the protocol directly. Track and plan registries are separate so registering one concern cannot accidentally mutate the other.

compiler.py is the configuration boundary. It chooses a WorkflowSpec; the selected plan factory then constructs its ordered tracks through the track registry.

execution.py runs primitive workflow payloads serially or in worker processes. It sits beside plans/ and tracks/ because it controls how a compiled workflow executes; the runner supplies input buffers and consumes ordered results.

docs.title: Runner layout
docs.text:
The default runner is split at runtime ownership boundaries:

Module Responsibility runner/run/default.py Validate a default annotation request and coordinate output and summary creation. runner/run/haplo.py Provide the vep run haplo verb. runner/run/stream.py Stream numbered buffers through workflow execution and preserve output order. runner/run/worker.py Own process-local sources, caches, workflow state, overlap attachment, and rendering. runner/run/output_transaction.py Stage and atomically commit output and summary files together. runner/run/progress.py Render parent-owned progress against the input variant count. 
flowchart LR
    Run["Runner
request lifecycle"] --> Transaction["OutputTransaction
stage and commit"]
    Run --> Stream["Buffer stream
ordered parent writer"]
    Stream --> Execution["Workflow execution
serial or processes"]
    Execution --> Worker["BufferedWorker
process-local runtime"]
    Worker --> Plan["WorkflowPlan
ordered tracks"]

This keeps Runner.run() readable in execution order and prevents process-local model and source state from leaking into file-management code. runner/run/__init__.py re-exports the default Runner, so existing Python API construction remains valid.

docs.title: Implemented path and extension points
docs.text:
The working command path is deliberately narrow today:

run.default -> default workflow -> transcript.consequence track

That path reads VCF input, retrieves complete GXF transcript graphs, finds transcript overlaps, calculates consequences, and writes annotated VCF records. It is the reference implementation for the package contracts described below.

compile_workflow_spec is the configuration boundary for this path. It translates run.default, or an empty command used by the Python API, into the default workflow and its one transcript.consequence track. It carries configured flank, overlap batch size, and readthrough values into the track specification. compile_workflow then delegates construction to the registered workflow and track factories. The buffered worker supplies live source, matcher, and annotator dependencies without naming registry entries itself.

Other names are extension points, not equivalent end-to-end features yet:

Extension Present today Still needed custom.default and custom.bigwig Custom feature and overlap contracts. Registered track factories, file-specific source integration, annotators, and output attachment. Colocated variants A colocated overlap finder. A configured source, track, annotator, and output integration in a runnable workflow. Regulatory features A regulatory overlap finder. A configured source, track, consequence path, and output integration in a runnable workflow. haplo Workflow and annotator registration scaffolding. Haplotype grouping, haplotype-specific interpretation, runner selection, and full output integration.

This distinction matters when adding configuration: a registered class or finder is not a supported track until the runner can construct its complete source-to-output path. Arbitrary track lists are intentionally not configuration yet; their schema should follow real second-track source, dependency, and output requirements rather than anticipate them.

docs.title: Runtime data flow
docs.text:
The runner transports primitive VCF buffer payloads to workers. A worker reconstructs model objects locally, then runs a WorkflowPlan over small annotation windows. The parent process is the only writer, so output remains in input order regardless of worker completion order.

sequenceDiagram
    participant Parent as Parent runner
    participant Worker as Worker-local runtime
    participant Resolver as Sequence-region resolver
    participant Buffer as InputBuffer
    participant Track as AnnotationTrack
    participant Source as Feature source and cache
    participant Output as Output writer

    Parent->>Worker: numbered payload with original VCF columns
    Worker->>Resolver: resolve uploaded region for this source
    Resolver-->>Worker: source name or unchanged uploaded name
    Worker->>Buffer: build allele interval index
    Worker->>Track: run each workflow track
    Track->>Source: retrieve candidate features
    Source-->>Track: complete source features
    Track->>Buffer: query candidate alleles by intervals
    Track->>Track: matcher then typed overlap then annotator
    Worker-->>Parent: numbered annotated lines and statistics delta
    Parent->>Output: write results in input order

The default output is variant_effect_output.txt, matching Perl VEP. The parent runner remains the only writer in every execution mode.

docs.title: Sequence-region names
docs.text:
Sequence-region resolution belongs to a source namespace. Runtime model slices are canonicalised to the reference FASTA namespace, while the uploaded VCF CHROM value is retained in the primitive payload and final output. GXF queries may need to translate that reference name back into the feature source's spelling. The current file source set therefore uses three separate resolvers:

  • uploaded VCF names to reference FASTA names;
  • raw GXF names to reference FASTA names while constructing transcript models;
  • reference model names back to indexed GXF names for regional transcript queries.

Explicit transcript aliases are reversed for the last direction, with ambiguous reversals rejected. Each resolver receives the names and aliases valid for its direction, then applies this order:

  1. Use an exact source name.
  2. Use an explicit alias.
  3. Add or remove the chr prefix and compare the candidate without case sensitivity.
  4. Keep the uploaded name unchanged when no source name matches.

Exact names therefore cannot be shadowed by an alias, and an explicit alias wins over the conventional chr adjustment. Resolution results are cached by the resolver instance.

The mapped name is used to construct model slices and query the source. The primitive input payload still carries the original VCF columns, including CHROM, ID, QUAL, and FILTER. Output starts from those columns, so source lookup never silently changes the uploaded record.

The default transcript track has three separate operations:

  1. Its candidate lookup queries the configured source around the input buffer and uses a worker-local BinnedFeatureCache for already-loaded transcripts.
  2. TranscriptOverlapFinder asks the InputBuffer interval index only for alleles in the transcript's influence interval. The influence interval includes the configured flank so that upstream and downstream consequences are not discarded during candidate discovery.
  3. The finder constructs a TranscriptVariationAllele (or structural equivalent) with the original transcript, then the consequence annotator evaluates it.

The distinction between influence interval and overlap model is intentional: a flank candidate is needed to decide upstream_gene_variant or downstream_gene_variant, but the model must still describe the real transcript span.

docs.title: Lifetimes and caches
docs.text:
An InputBuffer owns its interval index and never owns source state. The worker first uses an input buffer for the full primitive payload to prime transcript retrieval. It then creates smaller buffers, limited by annotation_window, for consequence calculation and rendering.

Only one window's workflow results and transient overlap graph are retained at a time. After its records are rendered, transcript variation allele links are cleared before the next window. This bounds graph memory independently of buffer_size; the primitive payload remains available until all its windows have been rendered without retaining every overlap model.

Worker-local state owns source handles, annotator contexts, and feature caches. A process builds these after it starts, rather than transporting open files, database connections, locks, or live model graphs. This is required for spawn and avoids relying on inherited mutable state with fork.

Feature caches are injected into candidate lookup rather than being global singletons:

  • IntervalTreeIndex indexes objects within one input buffer.
  • BinnedFeatureCache retains indexed transcript features for one process payload. It is cleared before the next payload so distant regions do not accumulate across a long-lived worker. An unindexed GXF is scanned again for each payload; a coordinate predicate filters transcript records before their model graphs are built or cached.
  • Sequence, mapper, codon, and zone-map caches have the lifetime required by their owning annotator context.

Cache use must never alter emitted annotations. Its purpose is to avoid repeated parsing, I/O, and coordinate work; it is not a second source of biological truth.

docs.title: DNA translation
docs.text:
common.codons.translate_dna uses the native Rust translation kernel when the PyO3 extension is available. The kernel performs the standard uppercase nuclear-codon lookup without crossing the Python boundary for each codon. If the optional extension cannot be imported, the same public function falls back to the Python codon table.

Both paths preserve the same contract: stop codons produce *, ambiguous, lowercase, and partial codons produce X, and translation continues after a stop codon. Tests cover both the native implementation and the Python fallback.

docs.title: Complete GXF transcript fetch
docs.text:
GFF3 and GTF transcript construction is a two-stage indexed operation when the source supports regional queries:

  1. Query the input region and identify overlapping transcript records and their complete spans.
  2. Query those full, merged spans and assemble transcript, exon, CDS, gene, and translation models from the returned records.

This matters because a narrow tabix query can find the transcript record near a variant while omitting distant exons or CDS records. The second query retains the full graph without building a whole-file graph in every worker. Sources without a usable region index fall back to a bounded sequential scan for each payload. Nonmatching transcript blocks are discarded before constructing Transcript, Gene, Exon, CDS, or Translation objects. This preserves memory bounds at the cost of repeated source scans. The sequential reader buffers one gene at a time, so every record for a gene must be contiguous; a source that revisits a previous gene requires an index for complete assembly. An indexed GXF remains strongly recommended for production workloads.

An unindexed FASTA follows the same correctness-over-speed principle. Length discovery scans its lines without retaining sequence, and a sequence request collects only the requested span. It never loads the whole reference into a worker, but repeated sequential scans are much slower than indexed random access. Production runs should supply a compatible FASTA index.

docs.title: Typed overlaps and results
docs.text:
An overlap finder produces a model appropriate to the feature pair:

  • TranscriptVariationAllele or TranscriptStructuralVariationAllele for transcript tracks;
  • CustomVariationAllele for custom records;
  • FeatureOverlap while regulatory and colocated-variant models are still generic.

CustomFeature.record holds source-native fields as dict[str, object]. File readers do not need to choose a global schema for BED, VCF, BigWig, or future formats. CustomVariationAllele stores format-neutral overlap geometry and optional summary_statistics; custom annotators decide how to interpret or render the source record.

AnnotationTrack returns TrackResult values that retain both the producing track identifier and the typed overlap. Result attachment happens after track execution, which makes independently run tracks safe to merge in deterministic order.

docs.title: Coordinate and insertion semantics
docs.text:
Intervals use 1-based inclusive coordinates. An insertion is represented as start = end + 1: a zero-width interbase point before start, rather than a changed reference base.

Candidate indexes expand an insertion to its two flanking bases only for retrieval. Matchers keep the interbase representation:

  • OverlapMatcher accepts containment in either direction and partial intersection. It supports contained, touching, and feature-relative three-prime insertion policies.
  • ExactCoordinateMatcher requires identical start and end, including two insertions at the same interbase point.
  • ReciprocalOverlapMatcher uses reference-span fractions and rejects zero-width insertions, whose reciprocal fraction is undefined.

CustomVariationAllele.overlap_length is consequently zero for an insertion. Its feature fraction is zero and its variation fraction is None, rather than an invented percentage. A caller that needs a point-association flag should use the matcher result, not a reference-base fraction.

docs.title: Execution modes
docs.text:
ExecutionSpec is independent of the workflow name. default and haplo workflows select track composition; execution options select how their input buffers run.

  • Serial: one worker runtime processes buffers directly. This is the reference path and has no process serialisation cost.
  • Spawn: each worker builds its sources, caches, and workflow from configuration after start. This is the portable process baseline.
  • Fork or forkserver: use the requested multiprocessing context, but still initialise worker-local runtime state explicitly. Do not depend on inherited open handles or warmed caches.
  • Track threads: WorkflowPlan.annotate(..., threads=N) may run independent tracks in a worker with up to N threads. Results are reassembled in declared track order.

Both spawn and fork process execution are opt-in; processes=1 is the default. Process workers consume numbered, serialisable buffers and return numbered results. A bounded in-flight queue and ordered collection keep output identical to input order even when later buffers finish first.

Threads are only for independent tracks, typically when their source calls are I/O-bound. They do not split one track or parallelise one consequence annotator, and they must not share mutable finder, source, or annotator state. The plan contract supports ordered independent tracks, but only the transcript track is runnable today. Per-track dependency ownership and isolation must be made concrete alongside the first additional runnable track; they are not implied by the current shared worker context. Every thread sees the same read-only input buffer.

Process-level buffer parallelism and track-level threading are orthogonal. Measure a real source mix before enabling either. Additional processes can improve throughput, but each worker has its own sources, feature cache, and annotation context, so the gain trades against aggregate memory. The current default workflow has one CPU-heavy consequence track; thread profiling did not show a gain, so threads=1 remains the default.

docs.title: Progress reporting
docs.text:
An interactive run shows completed VCF records against the exact input record count. The parent counts records in a bounded-memory first pass, then advances progress only after each ordered worker result is written. Workers never write progress themselves, so process completion order cannot scramble the terminal.

Progress is shown only when stderr is a terminal. --no_progress disables it explicitly and --quiet suppresses it together with informational logging. Redirected output therefore remains free of progress text. A multi-allelic VCF row counts once because the progress unit is an input variant record, matching the number of output rows.

On the 4,469,028-record ClinVar profiling input, the exact counting pass took 2.92 seconds on the development machine. It is therefore negligible beside consequence annotation, while non-terminal runs retain zero counting overhead.

docs.title: Extending the architecture
docs.text:
To add a new annotation track:

  1. Add or reuse a Feature model and a source that builds complete instances.
  2. Choose a cache and candidate-lookup callable with the correct worker lifetime.
  3. Reuse a matcher or add a small pure matcher under matcher/.
  4. Add a typed overlap model when pair-local geometry or state matters.
  5. Implement an OverlapFinder that constructs that model.
  6. Implement an Annotator that returns a typed result value.
  7. Register a TrackSpec.kind factory under workflow/tracks/ and select it from a plan under workflow/plans/.
  8. Test serial and threaded result equivalence, cache-disabled correctness, coordinate boundaries, and worker reconstruction under the supported process start methods.

Current extension points include additional track factories, custom source formats and annotators, specialised regulatory and colocated overlap models, and haplotype-specific track composition. The implementation-status table above identifies the work still required to make those runnable. A future configuration schema for several tracks and explicit per-track dependency ownership belong to that work. The present contracts allow it without moving retrieval or execution logic into annotators.

docs.title: Performance reasoning
docs.text:
The architecture is designed to make cost visible and local:

  • interval indexes replace repeated feature-by-allele scans;
  • binned feature caches avoid repeated indexed source reads across overlapping intervals within one process payload;
  • annotation windows release transient overlap graphs before the next window;
  • bounded process queues preserve input order without retaining the entire input;
  • bounded track batches avoid materialising every overlap in a large buffer.

Profiling should guide cache sizes, buffer sizes, annotation windows, process counts, and optional track threads. Keep measurements and source mixes with benchmark work; do not treat one machine's timing as a permanent architecture constant.

docs.title: Representative profiles
docs.text:
These measurements guided the current defaults. They are local observations, not performance guarantees. The representative slice contains 1,815 ClinVar records from chromosome 1. Runs used the indexed production GFF3 and FASTA named in the profiling command.

Profile Wall time or peak Conclusion 1,815-record, chromosome-1-derived ClinVar slice before native DNA translation 18.7 s Python translation was a material CPU cost. The same slice during native-kernel optimisation 11.6 s Moving the translation kernel removed about 38% in that run; the translation microbenchmark improved 5.8 times. Final single-process verification, default 5,000-record buffer 16.5 s; 631 MiB maximum resident set One payload cannot occupy a second process. Final single-process verification, 1,000-record buffers 19.3 s Smaller payloads add repeated source/cache setup. Final two-spawn-worker verification, 1,000-record buffers 10.6 s Buffer parallelism improved wall time by about 45%; emitted data lines were identical. Earlier aggregate-memory observation with two spawn workers ~925 MiB peak Process parallelism duplicates worker-local source, feature, and annotation state. Synthetic independent tracks with two threads 9.6% slower Thread scheduling did not help the measured workload. Synthetic independent tracks with four threads 28.7% slower More threads increased the regression. Exact full-input profile, stopped after 90 s 5,000 committed records; 246.8 million calls A complete profiled pass over 4,469,028 records would take many hours, so the bounded run was used to identify hot paths. Exact full-input memory observation ~939 MiB after 15,005 committed records Payload-scoped transcript state prevents growth across distant regions; one dense payload still has a substantial working set.

The final profile contains 81.4 million calls over 31.0 CPU-profiled seconds. Workflow annotation accounts for 21.3 seconds and the columnar-staged consequence strategy for 18.8 seconds, so the remaining hot work is consequence fact evaluation rather than buffer transport. The process result supports opt-in buffer parallelism when memory permits. The thread result does not rule out future I/O-heavy track mixes, but it does support a default of one thread and explicit measurement before changing it.

docs.title: Consequence annotators: developer guide
docs.text: How this codebase decides which Sequence Ontology (SO) consequence terms apply to a variant, and how to work on it without breaking anything.

docs.title: The idea in one paragraph
docs.text:
Ensembl VEP decides consequences with ~76 Perl predicate functions, 44 of which call each other to suppress themselves (104 call sites). Adding one splice term there means auditing five neighbouring function bodies. Here the same logic is split three ways: facts (named, cost-tagged, memoised properties of one variant-against-one-feature), rules (each SO term as a boolean formula over fact atoms, plus a declarative subsumes list), and annotators (interchangeable strategies that evaluate the rules). Suppression is declared on the winning term instead of being scattered through predicate bodies, so adding a term touches one catalogue record.

   facts                rules                          annotators
   ─────                ─────                          ──────────
   overlap_cds   ──┐    stop_gained =                  linear          ─┐
   partial_codon ──┼──►   overlap_cds                  staged           │
   is_snv        ──┤      & !partial_codon             columnar         ├──► list[OverlapConsequence]
   peptide_...   ──┘      & alt_peptide_has_ter       columnar-staged  │
                          & !ref_peptide_has_ter                      ─┘
   what is true         which term follows             how to work it out

The invariant that makes it safe: every annotator must produce byte-identical output. A new strategy is a candidate you diff against the incumbent, not a rewrite you have to trust.

docs.title: The two contexts
docs.text:
They are split by lifetime, and that is the only thing that distinguishes them.

  • context/fact.py — FactContext is one (variant, feature) overlap. It holds the fact memo table, the cost counters, and the uncharged shared intermediates (variant_span, biotype) that more than one fact would otherwise recompute.
  • context/annotator.py — AnnotatorContext is one annotation run. It holds every cache whose unit of reuse is bigger than a single overlap: the zone map, the shared-codon cache, and the candidate caches.

Sharing is opt-in and total. Construct one AnnotatorContext and pass it to every annotator that should share; pass nothing and each annotator gets a private, empty one. Whether caches are shared must never change the terms produced — that is what makes a cache safe to benchmark by turning it off, and it is asserted directly in tests/annotators/consequence/context/.

context = AnnotatorContext(codon_cache=CodonEditLRUCache(), zone_map_cache=ZoneMapCache())
annotator = ColumnarStagedAnnotator(annotator_context=context)

docs.title: The annotators
docs.text:
Every one produces identical terms. They differ only in how much work they avoid — and caches are orthogonal to the strategy, which is why there are five Python strategies rather than a cross-product of names.

Name What it does cost/ctx ms/1k consequence.linear VEP-faithful: cheap-guard digest, candidate cache, rank-ordered scan. The conformance reference. 196.3 48.9 consequence.columnar Bit-parallel over a batch. Cuts dispatch, not fact cost — note its cost/ctx ≈ linear's. 195.8 36.9 consequence.staged Cheap facts first, then propagate requires implications; expensive tier only when a rule is still undecided. 74.8 29.9 consequence.columnar-staged Columnar + requires propagation as bit-parallel forced-false masks. 73.9 19.5 (batch) consequence.columnar-kernels columnar-staged, with the cheap fact columns filled by native batch kernels. Only flat integer arrays cross FFI. 71.9 17.3 (batch)

The zone map and the shared-codon cache are not strategies — they are caches any strategy can be built with, so they multiply this table rather than extending it:

ColumnarStagedAnnotator(zone_map=ZoneMapCache(), codon_cache=CodonEditLRUCache())

A note on the regular.* names in this document. The strategy namespace was regular. before annotators/regular/ became annotators/consequence/strategies/. Live strategies were renamed with it (regular.linear → consequence.linear); retired ones — regular.zonemap, regular.columnar-staged-zonemap, every regular.rust-* — are left spelled as they were actually registered, since renaming them would invent names that never existed.

That combination is what used to be registered as regular.columnar-staged-zonemap; regular.zonemap was LinearFactsAnnotator(zone_map=ZoneMapCache()).

Because the caches are orthogonal to the strategy, the benchmark measures the combinations explicitly rather than relying on registry names: vep bench matrix crosses every strategy with the cache sets given by --caches, each with fresh caches. Heavy-locus, batched:

configuration cost/ctx ms/1k columnar-staged 73.9 19.5 columnar-staged + zone map 17.4 10.2 columnar-staged + zone map + codon cache 13.0 11.1 columnar-kernels + zone map 16.4 8.1 columnar-kernels + zone map + codon cache 12.0 9.0

The codon cache lowers cost/ctx and raises wall-clock in both pairs — the clearest illustration in the table of why both numbers are reported.

Numbers are heavy-locus corpus, --fuzz 4000 --repeats 3. cost/ctx is weighted fact computations; native annotators show 0.00 there because their facts are computed in Rust.

Two results worth internalising:

  • columnar-staged's cost/ctx exactly equals staged's (74.84 both). That is empirical proof that the one-pass topological forced-false sweep is bit-identical to the per-context implied_false fixpoint it replaces.
  • A native zone map bought nothing (14.73 vs 15.58 ms/1k — noise). Native fact costs flatten, so there are no expensive tiers left to avoid. The Python-side wins do not all survive a port.

docs.title: Add or remove an SO term
docs.text:
uv run vep catalogue add --dry_run --term my_term \
    --accession SO:0001234 --impact MODERATE --so_parent SO:0001060 --when '"overlap_cds"'
uv run vep catalogue remove --term my_term --catalogue <path>

It derives subsumes from SO parentage (if A is_a B, then A is more specific, so A subsumes B), cleans up dangling subsumes references on removal, renumbers ranks, and validates before writing.

It will not invent a when formula. That is deliberate: a plausible-looking wrong rule passes conformance — every annotator agrees on the same wrong answer — and only surfaces later as bad biology. The script suggests candidate fact atoms and makes you author the rule.

docs.title: Naming a fact: the relation vocabulary
docs.text:
Positional facts name the relation between the variant's span and the thing it is tested against, using one of four prefixes. Pick the one that is literally true of the predicate body:

Prefix Meaning within_ the variant lies entirely inside the feature contain_ the variant entirely contains the feature intersect_ partial overlap — each side has a non-overlapped part overlap_ any overlap at all (the union of the three above)

So overlap_feature (any overlap with the overlapped feature), contain_feature (the variant swallows it whole), overlap_cds, overlap_exon, overlap_donor_site, and so on. The noun is the thing tested against, and feature — not transcript — is correct wherever the body only reads Feature.start/Feature.end, because those facts hold for a Motif or Regulatory feature just as they do for a Transcript.

overlap_five_prime_utr and overlap_three_prime_utr used to be the exception (in_five_prime_utr/ in_three_prime_utr, not genuine overlap tests) but no longer are — see their docstrings in consequence/facts/position.py for what they used to compute, the model bug that made the old names honest, and why fixing both was a semantic change rather than a rename.

docs.title: Naming a non-boolean helper
docs.text: Not everything in consequence/facts/ is a boolean rule atom — a fact's body often needs a non-boolean intermediate (a footprint, a peptide pair, a set of nearby intron windows), and the question of whether that intermediate should be @fact-decorated (memoised, cost-tracked, underscore-prefixed) or a plain helper function is a different one from the vocabulary above. See the module docstring of consequence/facts/base.py for the four categories and the eligibility/promotion rule — that module is the source of truth; this section only points at it so the rule is not duplicated and cannot drift. Every plain helper (categories 3 and 4) lives in consequence/facts/helper.py, not next to the boolean facts that call it; visibility there is controlled by __all__ alone, not by a leading underscore.

docs.title: Add a fact
docs.text:
Facts are grouped by what question they answer: kind.py (what kind of feature/variant this is), position.py (coordinate comparison), sequence.py (sequence/peptide content or length arithmetic). Register a new fact in whichever one matches, with a cost tier and, if it is genuinely gated on another fact, a requires declaration:

@fact(CostTier.MAPPING, deps=("overlap_exon",), requires=("overlap_exon",))
def my_new_fact(fact_context): ...

deps = must be computed first. requires = must be true first — that is the implication the staged strategies exploit to settle rules without computing anything.

requires is enforced by the decorator, not by you. The body runs only when every required atom is already true, so do not open it with if not get_fact(ctx, "overlap_exon"): return False — that is dead code, and hand-writing the guard next to the declaration is exactly how the two used to drift. requires names are folded into deps automatically too, so declare each one once.

docs.title: When a term cannot be a boolean formula
docs.text:
Some VEP predicates genuinely resist boolean expression (data-dependent loops, non-boolean intermediates). fact does not require the body to be a formula composed from other atoms — it takes an arbitrary compute function — so there is no separate mechanism for this case, just an ordinary fact:

@fact(CostTier.BOUNDS)
def my_bespoke_check(fact_context):
    for exon in fact_context.transcript.spliced_exons:  # arbitrary control flow
        ...

Reference it from when exactly like any other atom — a bare "my_bespoke_check", or {"all": ["my_bespoke_check", ...]} alongside other conjuncts. One hard rule: such a fact may read other facts (via get_fact) but must never call another fact's compute function directly — that cross-calling is the VEP coupling this design exists to remove; going through get_fact keeps memoisation, cost accounting, and subsumes/prune's "adding a term touches one record" property intact regardless of how opaque a body's internals are. Declare cost/deps/requires honestly, same as any fact — every strategy (staging, zone maps, cheap-guard) reasons from those, not from whether the body happens to look like a formula, so an opaque fact loses nothing by being opaque as long as it is priced and gated truthfully.

An earlier revision had a dedicated predicate decorator and a {"predicate": "name"} JSON sugar form purely to flag this case as greppable; both were removed as unneeded machinery over what a plain fact reference already does.

docs.title: Add an annotator
docs.text:
Subclass ConsequenceAnnotator[FactRuleSet], implement annotate_feature_overlap, decorate with @register_annotator("consequence.my_strategy"), and import it from consequence/strategies/__init__.py. Conformance and the benchmark auto-discover registered names — you get both for free.

Call self.annotator_context.prepare(fact_context) once per overlap, before computing any fact, and your strategy supports both caches with no further work. Register a name only for a genuinely different evaluation strategy — if the difference is "with a cache attached", that is a constructor argument, not a strategy.

docs.title: Push a fact into a native batch kernel
docs.text:
consequence.columnar-kernels is the second, deliberately different bet on Rust. Where the regular.rust-* annotators move the whole annotator native — and so have to mirror a NativeTranscript across the boundary and keep it in step with the model — the kernels in src/rust/annotators/ruleset/batch_kernels.rs take flat integer arrays and nothing else. They do not know what a transcript is, and "do these two closed intervals overlap" will never grow a field.

To add one: write the kernel taking Vec<i64> and returning a packed little-endian bitmap, export it in lib.rs, and have your annotator's seed_columns marshal the arrays and hand back {fact_name: int.from_bytes(bitmap, "little")}.

The one rule that decides whether it pays: only seed facts that nothing reads through get_fact from inside another fact's body. Seeding a column is nearly free; fanning results back into per-overlap memos costs ~750 ns/context and eats the entire win. See the measured breakdown below.

docs.title: Handle more than one feature class
docs.text: build_fact_ruleset() takes no feature kind: one rule set covers every class, with no per-class subset to select. A rule restricted to one class says so in its own formula, via the FREE class facts in consequence/facts/kind.py (is_transcript, is_motif, is_regulatory, is_structural) — e.g. {"all": ["is_regulatory", "overlap_feature"]}. FactRule.cheap_guard (rules/rulesets.py) picks up that conjunct automatically, so an interleaved stream of Transcript and Regulatory overlaps settles the wrong-class rules on a type check without a separate masking pass. See columnar.py's own comment on why this needs no per-rule feature-class masking.

docs.title: Debug why a term did or did not appear
docs.text:
uv run vep corpus describe --kind default                 # what is in the corpus, and every selectable overlap
uv run vep explain --annotator consequence.staged --index 40
uv run vep explain --compare consequence.staged,consequence.linear --index 40
uv run vep explain --name ENST0001_cds3_del1 --graph svg --output_file derivation.html
uv run vep explain --variant chrSynthetic:3005:ACG>- --transcript ENST0001

Shows each fact's origin (computed / prefilled by zone map / codon-cache hit / forced False by requires) and how often it was read, per-rule verdicts with the reason they were settled, the pruning chain, and the emitted terms. --compare diffs two annotators and reports the first divergence — the tool you want the day a conformance test fails. An overlap is selected by --name, by --index, or by --variant CHR:POS:REF>ALT (with - for an empty allele) plus --transcript when several features share it; vep corpus describe lists all three for every overlap, and explain --list is the short form of that listing. The SVG graph format writes a linked HTML document with emitted terms first, pruned terms next, and non-firing terms last. Each term keeps its Boolean expression: blue nodes evaluated true, red nodes evaluated false, and white nodes were not observed.

Tracing is opt-in and costs nothing when off. The annotation path records only what a later pass cannot recover — per-fact read counts, and which cache served which fact — so get_fact pays one is not None check and nothing else; origins, costs, forced-False facts and rule verdicts are all derived afterwards by trace/reconstruct.py. tests/trace/test_conformance.py is the gate on that derivation matching the run it claims to explain.

The native annotators never trace, by design — since all are byte-identical, debug with a Python twin and you get the same answer.

docs.title: See the corpus the tests run against
docs.text:
uv run vep corpus save --kind both --corpus_dir /tmp/corpus     # corpus.fa, corpus.gff3, corpus.vcf, manifest.json
uv run vep corpus describe --kind heavy --format markdown

save writes the synthetic corpus as the files a real run reads, in the conventions the GFF3/VCF transcript and variation readers expect, with the generator's variant name in the VCF ID column. Loading it back is not a corpus verb: it is --input_file corpus.vcf --gff corpus.gff3 --fasta corpus.fa on any command, which waits on the file-backed overlap source. Until then every file still round-trips through the existing parsers (tests/corpus/test_store.py). describe shows chromosomes, transcripts, variant classes, how many distinct transcripts a batch chunk touches, and the overlap listing.

docs.title: Summarise a run, or profile the facts
docs.text:
uv run vep stats --input_file annotated.vcf --format html --output_file summary.html
uv run vep stats --profile --kind default --annotator consequence.staged --format text

Two planes, kept as two types on purpose. The run summary (stats/summary.py, RunSummary) is term-level and cheap -- about a microsecond an overlap -- so run writes it by default alongside its output, and vep stats --input_file rebuilds the same summary from any annotated VCF, ours or another tool's: output/parser/vcf.py reads the CSQ/ANN layout out of the header and seeds each allele's consequences directly, so it needs no --gff/--fasta, and Variation.most_severe_consequence / .class_so_term answer with zero transcripts attached. The fact profile (trace/run.py, RunTrace) is fact-level and measurably slower, so it is opt-in behind --profile; it says what every fact cost a run, how often it was read, and what the caches and requires propagation saved. Both satisfy one Reportable Protocol (stats/report.py) and go through one renderer (render/report.py), so --format html|text|json never branches on which it was handed.

The profile report names the cost table it used. --fact_cost_override rewrites every fact's declared cost process-wide and never restores it, so two profiles are only comparable when that line agrees.

docs.title: Gotchas
docs.text:
• Bare cargo test aborts with SIGABRT. The debug test binary cannot resolve libpython3.10.dylib. Always prefix DYLD_FALLBACK_LIBRARY_PATH=/Users/snhossain/miniconda3/lib.
  • validate_consequence_ruleset.py now exits 0. It used to report feature_truncation as a dead rule: the prototype's inherited formula was contain_feature & decreases_length & !is_deletion, and decreases_length and is_deletion are the same formula, so it was mathematically unreachable. The contradictory conjunct has no counterpart in the Perl and is gone; the rule now carries is_structural instead, which is the declarative form of VEP's return 0 if $bvfoa->isa('...TranscriptVariationAllele'). A non-zero exit is now a real failure.
  • Conformance is the gate, not a nicety. Any new strategy must be byte-identical to consequence.linear on both corpora before its timings mean anything.
  • cost/ctx and ms/1k rank strategies differently on purpose. cost/ctx measures the strategy; ms/1k measures this Python process. They disagree, and that disagreement is the point.
  • The declared cost tiers are a model, not truth. Declared 0/1/5/20/60; measured Python is nearly flat, and native code inverts the order (a coordinate map costs ~4x a codon translate). They rank strategies correctly; do not treat them as absolute.
  • At a PyO3 boundary, what you return costs more than how often you cross. Batching alone bought 1.08x; switching the return payload from term strings to u16 indices bought 3.48x.
  • Skipping a rule because something suppresses it is not sound on its own. prune() drops a term whenever any hit term subsumes it — and a hit term that is itself dropped still contributes its own subsumes. So eliding a suppressed rule loses whatever that rule would have suppressed. Concretely: splice_donor_region_variant suppresses splice_region_variant; skip splice_region_variant and coding_transcript_variant wrongly survives. A rule may only be skipped when its own subsumes are already covered.

docs.title: Measured negative results
docs.text:
Kept deliberately, so they are not rediscovered at cost.

  • A native zone map bought nothing (14.73 vs 15.58 ms/1k — noise). Native fact costs flatten, so there are no expensive tiers left to avoid.
  • Native optimisation machinery does not pay at all. regular.rust-naive — every rule evaluated one by one, no staging, no zone map, no bit-parallelism — matches the fully optimised regular.rust-columnar-staged-zonemap (4.177 vs 4.182 ms/1k batched). The ~10.8x native speedup is entirely the FFI boundary shape (batched calls returning u16 indices), not the strategy.
  • Subsumes-topological early skipping is a small net loss. StagedFactsAnnotator(early_subsumption_skip=True) measured 28.81 → 29.07 ms/1k (boundary+fuzz) and 30.66 → 31.30 (heavy-locus), skipping only 2–3% of rule evaluations. Staging has already settled most suppressed rules cheaply, and the soundness condition above makes the skip much narrower than it looks. Off by default; the code and its tests are kept for the soundness trap, not the speed.
  • The shared-codon cache is a small wall-clock loss in Python (35.71 → 36.73 ms/1k) despite a 91.6% hit rate — building the key costs more than the work it saves.
  • Porting scalar primitives to Rust is worthless; porting column kernels pays ~1.2x. Two separate findings from the same experiment:
  • genomic_overlap is 4.6% of the no-zone-map path and 0.0% with a zone map attached — the zone map already eliminates that whole family in pure Python, for free. There is nothing left for a native genomic_overlap to win.
  • At kernel granularity, PyO3 is slower than Python at the arithmetic itself: 48.5 µs vs 28.4 µs for six variant-shape facts over a 256-context chunk. Converting a Python list to Vec<i64> and back dominates completely; the comparisons are noise. A kernel only pays if it displaces dispatch, not arithmetic.
  • consequence.columnar-kernels nonetheless measures 1.15–1.24x over consequence.columnar-staged (17.3 vs 19.5 ms/1k batched), because seeding eight fact columns removes ~2,000 get_fact calls per chunk. It cuts facts/ctx from 23.9 to 15.9 — a third of all fact computations — for a 1.2x wall-clock win, which is the clearest statement anywhere in this repo that the cost is dispatch, not facts.
  • An earlier version that also prefilled every seeded fact into the per-overlap memos measured 1.01x — dead even. The per-context fan-out is ~750 ns/context against ~190 ns for the kernel call. Column-only seeding is the whole difference between the two results.
  • The same lesson applied to the zone map is worth more than the Rust was, and needs no Rust. The zone map used to prefill its 16 facts into each overlap's memo, after which a columnar annotator still called get_fact once per (fact, overlap) to read them back — ~800k calls on the heavy-locus corpus, all memo hits. ZoneMapCache.columns returns them as bit columns instead; only the five named in MEMO_FACT_NAMES (those some other fact's requires guard reads) still need to exist per overlap. 13.16 → 10.42 ms/1k, a 1.26x win in pure Python.
  • Profiling answers "should the zone-map bisect be batched in Rust?" with: not on its own. ZoneMap.lookup — the bisect plus mask OR — is 3.9% of the fastest configuration's runtime, so a free native version caps out there. The whole of ZoneMapCache.columns is 16.1%, and the bisect is a quarter of it; the rest is the per-context Python loop that decodes 16 bits, applies the flank suppression and recomputes the UTR pair. Porting that is the ~13% opportunity, and it is still flat-array-shaped (zone starts, masks, inverted triples, bounds, utr_test) so it would not rot. The catch is batching: chunks average 18 distinct transcripts per 256 overlaps on the heavy-locus corpus, so it needs CSR-style arrays or a stateful native handle holding the maps — per-transcript calls of ~14 contexts are far too small to amortise PyO3's list conversion.

docs.title: Direct Python-object access from Rust (measured)
docs.text:
RustNaiveAnnotator.direct_transcript_access = True makes Rust read the Python Transcript attribute by attribute (annotate_batch_indices_direct in src/rust/annotators/consequence/strategies/naive.rs) instead of being handed a NativeTranscript built and cached on the Python side. It deletes the Python-side mirror — the hand-listed field extraction in annotators/rust/base.py that is the part of the native port most likely to fall behind the model.

corpus mirror direct access boundary+fuzz (4 transcripts) 4.43 ms/1k (10.98x) 4.66 ms/1k (10.44x) heavy-locus (36 transcripts) 5.32 ms/1k (9.96x) 6.15 ms/1k (8.62x)

It costs 5–16%, and you keep 8.6–10.4x. Much cheaper than it looks, because the adapter already groups a chunk by transcript, so extraction happens once per (chunk, transcript) group rather than per context — ~3.5k extractions instead of 36 on heavy-locus, not 50k.

The spread between the corpora is the amortisation: the mirror is built once per transcript for the annotator's lifetime, so the more variants share a transcript the better it looks. heavy-locus has 1,404 variants per transcript and loses 16%; boundary+fuzz has ~870 across only 4 transcripts and loses 5%. A corpus with few variants per transcript would favour direct access outright.

  • docs/developer_guide/ — this guide.
  • Module docstrings carry the real reasoning; caches/zone_map.py, consequence/strategies/columnar_staged.py and caches/codon_cache.py in particular explain invariants that are easy to break.
