docs.title: Edited boundaries: rebuilding the CDS around a variant
docs.text:
How TranscriptVariationAllele._full_cds_alleles decides where the coding sequence starts and ends once a variant has been applied — and why one four-line function handles the start boundary, the end boundary, insertions and deletions without a single special case.

Companion to Consequence annotators; the facts that consume this are cds_start_lost, cds_stop_lost, cds_start_retained and cds_stop_retained in annotators/consequence/facts/sequence.py.

docs.title: The problem
docs.text:
The reference CDS is easy: spliced_seq[cdna0 : cdna0 + cds_length], where cdna0 is the CDS start as a 0-based offset into the spliced transcript. The alternate is not, because applying an edit moves the ground under both of those offsets.

The edit is modelled uniformly — replace the half-open offset range [edit_start, edit_end) with the strand-corrected alternate allele — and applied to spliced_seq, the whole 5'UTR + CDS + 3'UTR in transcript sense. delta is the net length change. Introns never appear, because transcript_mapper is block-overlap based over the real exon list, so intronic bases map to no offset at all: splicing is always assumed to proceed normally.

Naively reusing cdna0 and cdna0 + cds_length against the edited sequence is wrong in two opposite directions:

  • A deletion upstream of the CDS slides the whole CDS left. Read at the old cdna0 and you start several bases into the coding sequence.
  • A deletion that destroys the start codon has no CDS start to speak of any more. Fall back to the old offset and you silently anchor into leftover 5'UTR, inventing a start that was deleted.

Both boundaries need the same treatment, so both go through one function.

docs.title: The function
docs.text:
def _edited_boundary(boundary0: int, edit_start: int, edit_end: int, delta: int) -> int:
    if boundary0 < edit_start:      # edit lies AFTER the boundary
        return boundary0
    if boundary0 >= edit_end:       # edit lies BEFORE the boundary
        return boundary0 + delta
    return edit_start               # edit STRADDLES the boundary

Called twice, and the result used as a plain slice:

anchor    = _edited_boundary(cdna0,    edit_start, edit_end, delta)
end_bound = _edited_boundary(cds_end0, edit_start, edit_end, delta)
alternate_cds = _nucleotide_sequence_up_to_stop(alternate_spliced_seq[anchor:end_bound])

docs.title: The three cases
docs.text:
A miniature transcript throughout: 4 bases of 5'UTR, a 9-base CDS, 4 bases of 3'UTR. cdna0 = 4; cds_end0 = 13 (exclusive, so it points at the first 3'UTR base).

  offset    01234567890123456
  spliced   uuuuATGGGGTAAnnnn
                ▲        ▲
              cdna0=4  cds_end0=13

docs.title: Case 1 — edit lies after the boundary → unchanged
docs.text:
Nothing upstream of the boundary moved, so its offset is still correct.

  spliced   uuuuATGGGGTAAnnnn        delete offsets 7-9 ("GGG")
                ▲  ───               edit = [7,10)   delta = -3
              cdna0=4

  edited    uuuuATGTAAnnnn
                ▲                    anchor = 4  (unchanged)

docs.title: Case 2 — edit lies before the boundary → slides by delta
docs.text:
The boundary still points at the same base; only its number changed. This is the case that looks alarming and is not: the anchor moves precisely because the sequence moved with it.

  spliced   uuuuATGGGGTAAnnnn        delete offsets 1-2 ("uu")
             ── ▲                    edit = [1,3)    delta = -2
                cdna0=4

  edited    uuATGGGGTAAnnnn
              ▲                      anchor = 2  ( = 4 + (-2) )

docs.title: Case 3 — edit straddles the boundary → collapses to edit_start
docs.text:
The boundary no longer exists in the edited sequence — the bases that defined it are gone. The only defensible answer is the edit itself.

  spliced   uuuuATGGGGTAAnnnn        delete offsets 3-5 ("uAT")
               ───                   edit = [3,6)    delta = -3
                ▲                    cdna0=4 falls inside the edit

  edited    uuuGGGGTAAnnnn
               ▲                     anchor = 3  ( = edit_start )

The same three cases apply unchanged to cds_end0; only the numbers differ.

  Case 1 (end)   delete offsets 14-15, in the 3'UTR   →  end_bound = 13  (unchanged)
  Case 2 (end)   delete offsets 7-9,  inside the CDS  →  end_bound = 10  ( = 13 - 3 )
  Case 3 (end)   delete offsets 11-14, stop + 1 UTR   →  end_bound = 11  ( = edit_start )

docs.title: Why one return value does opposite things at each end
docs.text:
Case 3 returns edit_start for both boundaries, but anchor and end_bound are the two ends of a slice — inclusive lower, exclusive upper. The same number therefore has opposite meanings, which is exactly what is wanted at each end.

  STRADDLING THE START — replace offsets 3-5 with "XXXXX"

  edited    uuuXXXXXGGGGTAAnnnn
               ▲
             anchor = 3, an INCLUSIVE lower bound
             → alternate_cds = XXXXXGGGGTAA…    reads THROUGH the replacement


  STRADDLING THE END — replace offsets 11-14 with "XXXXX"

  edited    uuuuATGGGGTXXXXXnn
                       ▲
                   end_bound = 11, an EXCLUSIVE upper bound
             → alternate_cds = ATGGGGT          stops BEFORE the replacement

Biologically that is the right pair of answers. An edit landing on the start codon replaces it, and whatever it puts there is what a ribosome would encounter first — so read it in. An edit landing on the stop codon destroys it, and nothing downstream can be trusted to be coding any more — so stop short. Neither case ever falls back into untouched UTR.

docs.title: Insertions can never straddle
docs.text:
For a pure insertion edit_start == edit_end, which makes the straddle branch's range edit_start <= boundary0 < edit_end empty. Case 3 is unreachable for insertions — structurally, not by convention. An insertion sits between two bases, so it is always cleanly before or after any boundary, and only Cases 1 and 2 ever fire.

  spliced   uuuuATGGGGTAAnnnn        insert "AAA" at offset 7
                ▲  ∧                 edit = [7,7)    delta = +3
              cdna0=4                the insertion is a zero-width point, so
                                     cdna0 = 4 < 7 → Case 1, anchor unchanged

Deletions and delins are the only edits that can destroy a boundary, which is why every straddle-case test in the suite is a deletion or a delins.

docs.title: The whole model in four lines
docs.text:
Because both boundaries are resolved against the same edit, the width of the window falls out correctly on its own:

Edit location anchor end_bound Net effect on the CDS Entirely 5' of the CDS +delta +delta window slides, width unchanged → identical CDS Entirely 3' of the CDS unchanged unchanged window untouched → identical CDS Inside the CDS unchanged +delta width changes by exactly delta Straddling a boundary = edit_start = edit_start that end re-anchors on the edit

Verified against the real fixture (cdna0 = 9, cds_end0 = 45):

Edit Range delta anchor end_bound alt == ref deletion in 5'UTR [2,6) −4 5 41 yes deletion straddling start [7,12) −5 7 40 no deletion inside CDS [14,18) −4 9 41 no deletion straddling end [42,46) −4 9 42 no deletion in 3'UTR [50,54) −4 9 45 yes insertion in 5'UTR [5,5) +3 12 48 yes insertion inside CDS [15,15) +3 9 48 no insertion in 3'UTR [50,50) +3 9 45 yes

A variant that touches no exon at all (purely intronic, or entirely outside the transcript) never reaches this machinery — genomic_span_to_cds_offsets returns None and the property short-circuits to (reference_cds, reference_cds), the same no-op a UTR-only edit arrives at by actually applying the edit. None is returned only when the transcript has no CDS at all.

docs.title: Opt-in readthrough
docs.text:
Everything above describes the default. A run may model what happens downstream of a destroyed stop codon by raising Readthrough (common/enums.py), which changes exactly one thing — the end_bound half of the table above:

Readthrough end_bound Reads NONE (default) _edited_boundary(cds_end0, …) the CDS only UTR len(alternate_spliced_seq) on into the 3'UTR, still inside the transcript BEYOND_TRANSCRIPT as UTR, then bounded flanking sequence past the transcript, from slice.seq

An IntEnum, so the levels are ordered rather than independent: BEYOND_TRANSCRIPT extends UTR, which makes "read past the transcript but not through the UTR" unrepresentable.

It is not gated on "was the stop actually lost?", deliberately. An intact, in-frame stop terminates translation wherever the bound sits, so raising the level is provably a no-op for every variant that leaves the stop alone — the levels can only diverge when no in-frame stop remains inside the coding sequence. That is what makes the option safe to switch on globally, and it is pinned by a test.

The level lives on the overlap, not on the call:

readthrough: Readthrough = field(
    default=Readthrough.NONE,
    on_setattr=invalidates("_full_cds_alleles", "_full_peptide_alleles"),
)

A parameterised cds_alleles(*, readthrough=…) was tried first and rejected: reference_cds and friends would keep answering at the default level while the fact layer asked for another, so one object would hold two disagreeing answers. As a field there is one cached value, every accessor agrees, and invalidates(...) makes reassignment recompute rather than serve a stale cache. AnnotatorContext.readthrough carries the run-scoped setting and prepare() stamps it onto each overlap before the sequence tier is reached — the same ordering rule the codon cache already depends on. Nothing in facts/sequence.py knows the option exists.

docs.title: Gotchas
docs.text:
• Translation is bounded by end_bound, never by "the next stop codon anywhere". It stops at the first in-frame stop within the window, or at end_bound if there is none. By default it does not read into the 3'UTR looking for a replacement stop, and does not read past the transcript. A stop-losing edit therefore yields an alternate peptide with no * — a legitimate answer, not an error. That default can be lifted per run; see Opt-in readthrough above.
  • cds_stop_lost checks the reference's own stop position, not "is there a stop anywhere". A frameshift can leave a coincidental in-frame * elsewhere; treating that as the stop being retained is wrong. The facts compare alternate_peptide[reference_stop] specifically, and require the prefix up to that point to match.
  • An insertion exactly at cds_end0 is currently treated as inside the CDS (Case 2, 13 >= 13), the mirror of an insertion at cdna0 being treated as 5'UTR. For a well-formed CDS this is masked entirely — the window still ends with the reference's own stop codon, so _nucleotide_sequence_up_to_stop truncates there and the inserted bases never survive. It would only surface on a CDS with no terminal stop (cds_end_NF-style incomplete annotation).
  • delta must be computed from spliced-transcript offsets, not the genomic span. A deletion whose genomic span crosses an intron removes fewer transcript bases than its genomic length suggests; genomic_span_to_cds_offsets already accounts for this, which is why every offset here is transcript-wide rather than CDS-relative.

docs.title: Splice hypotheses: intron retention and exon skipping
docs.text:
Designed but not implemented — the design, the constraints found while producing it, and the verification gate are written up in Splice hypotheses.

Both events reduce to "a different ordered list of Features making up the mature transcript", so they reuse the existing edit arithmetic rather than adding a parallel copy of it. Scoped as informational output only: the SO terms stay on the normal splicing model, which is what keeps every cache key valid and makes byte-identical consequence output the acceptance gate. Its sibling feature, opt-in stop-codon readthrough, has landed; see Edited boundaries.

docs.title: The structural-variant class model
docs.text:
Four terms — TFBS_ablation, TFBS_amplification, regulatory_region_ablation, regulatory_region_amplification — are implemented, but with an approximation that should be revisited once the model layer can express a CNV class.

VEP's feature_amplification is complete_overlap_feature and copy_number_gain, and copy_number_gain is duplication, tandem repeat, or a gain-flavoured class SO term. Likewise deletion's structural branch and copy_number_loss. models/variation/structural_variation_allele.py carries no class_so_term and there is no _supporting_cnv_terms equivalent, so the rules currently use increases_length/decreases_length gated on is_structural in their place.

That is narrower than VEP's condition, not wrong: every variant these fire on genuinely qualifies, but a CNV expressed purely as a class SO term (with no length change) will be missed. Closing the gap needs StructuralVariationAllele.class_so_term plus its supporting-CNV terms, and then facts for copy_number_gain/copy_number_loss.

Note also that Motif and Regulatory are still empty stubs (Feature subclasses with no fields), and there is no dedicated Motif/Regulatory overlap class — a plain FeatureOverlap is used. That is sufficient for the positional and containment rules, which read only start/end, but anything needing motif-relative position (a real TFBS_amplification score, say) will need them fleshed out.

docs.title: overlap_five_prime_utr / overlap_three_prime_utr are not overlap tests
docs.text:
They keep the older in_ prefix rather than the within_/contain_/intersect_/overlap_ vocabulary, because they are genuinely not interval-overlap tests: the current definition is "overlap_exon anywhere in the span and the span's low (or high) end lies beyond the CDS bound", which fires for a forward-strand variant running from an intron into the CDS even though it touches no UTR base. See the module docstring of consequence/facts/position.py.

Redefining them as genuine overlap_five_prime_utr/overlap_three_prime_utr predicates would let them be served straight from the zone mask like every other positional fact, removing the last special case in ZoneMapCache.prefill. It is a semantic change and has to be checked against VEP's intent, which is why it was kept out of the rename.

docs.title: transcript_amplification and mature_miRNA_variant
docs.text: Still on EXCLUDED_TERMS with no when. transcript_amplification is the same feature_amplification predicate as the regulatory pair and could be added on the same terms; mature_miRNA_variant needs miRNA attributes and a cDNA-coordinate mapper that the model layer does not have.

docs.title: Early pruning does not pay (item 7)
docs.text:
Implemented as StagedFactsAnnotator(early_subsumption_skip=True), off by default.

Corpus off on boundary+fuzz (3,476) 28.81 ms/1k 29.07 ms/1k 0.99x heavy-locus (50,544) 30.66 ms/1k 31.30 ms/1k 0.98x

Only 2–3% of rule evaluations are skipped. Both reasons for scepticism held: staging has already settled most suppressed rules cheaply, and the subsumption graph's rank inversions are real.

The valuable part was a soundness bug found in the first attempt: skipping a rule merely because something suppresses it is wrong. prune() drops a term whenever any hit term subsumes it, and a hit term that is itself dropped still contributes its own subsumes — so eliding splice_region_variant (suppressed by splice_donor_region_variant) let coding_transcript_variant wrongly survive. A rule may be skipped only when its own subsumes are already covered. The code and tests/annotators/consequence/rules/test_subsumes_order.py are kept for that trap, not the timing.

The contradictory conjunct has no counterpart in the Perl and is gone. The validator now exits 0, so a non-zero exit is a real failure.

docs.title: Splice hypotheses: intron retention and exon skipping
docs.text: Status: designed, not implemented. Nothing described here exists in the code yet. Its sibling feature, opt-in stop-codon readthrough (Readthrough), is implemented — see Edited boundaries. This page records the design and, more importantly, the constraints and reasoning behind it, so whoever picks it up does not have to re-derive them.

docs.title: The problem
docs.text:
The CDS reconstruction assumes splicing proceeds normally: introns are never candidate sequence, every annotated exon is used. That is the right default and it should stay the default — the actual outcome of a disrupted splice site (retention vs. exon skipping vs. a cryptic site) is not predictable from sequence alone, which is why VEP treats splice disruption as a qualitative consequence (splice_donor_variant) rather than something to reconstruct sequence for.

But "if this donor site is destroyed and intron 3 is retained, what protein comes out?" is a real question, and today there is no way to ask it.

docs.title: Decisions taken
docs.text:
Three, agreed before design, and they shape everything below:

  1. Informational output only. SO terms keep being computed on the normal model. A hypothesis produces additional sequence/peptide output for reporting; it never changes a consequence.
  2. The caller names the event explicitly — "retain intron 3", "skip exon 4". Nothing is inferred from the splice facts.
  3. Both events behind one SpliceModel, rather than two separate features.

Decision (1) is load-bearing, and it dissolves two hazards that made this look expensive when it was first deferred:

  • No cache key changes. CodonEditKey.build is built from transcript.mapper — the CDS spans of the normal model — which a hypothesis never touches. Same for ZoneMapCache ((stable_id, version)) and MapperIndexCache (stable_id). Had hypotheses fed the facts, every one of those keys would have needed the model folding in, or silently shared results between hypotheses — precisely the under-inclusion failure caches/codon_cache.py's docstring warns about.
  • A method taking the model is the right shape here. For readthrough it was a trap: the level had to be a field, because alternate_cds and the fact layer would otherwise report different levels from one object. A hypothesis is a separate, differently-named output, so that failure mode does not arise.

docs.title: The key insight
docs.text:
Everything the reconstruction needs — mapper, sequence, coding start, coding end — derives from one ordered list of Features making up the mature transcript. The default model is exactly transcript.spliced_exons. So:

  normal         exon0 ─────── exon1 ─────── exon2
                       (intron0)     (intron1)

  retain intron0 exon0 ─ intron0 ─ exon1 ─────── exon2      <- insert one Feature
  skip exon1     exon0 ───────────────────────── exon2      <- drop one Feature

No other special case is needed, because Feature._seq already returns transcript-sense sequence for a slice-relative span. Its docstring says so explicitly: it exists precisely so callers can concatenate a list of child features in 5'->3' order without handling strand themselves — the contract Transcript._spliced_seq already relies on.

Coding boundaries come back by mapping genomic positions, which are invariant under a splicing hypothesis, through the modified mapper:

cdna0    = min(modified_mapper.genomic_to_cds_offset(p) for p in start_codon_genomic_spans())
cds_end0 = max(modified_mapper.genomic_to_cds_offset(p) for p in stop_codon_genomic_spans()) + 1

Taking min/max over mapped offsets is strand-agnostic, since offsets are always transcript-sense. And if a skipped exon contains the ATG the mapping returns None, so "no start codon" falls out for free rather than needing a branch.

docs.title: Design sketch
docs.text:
class SpliceEvent(Enum):          # common/enums.py
    RETAIN_INTRON = "retain_intron"
    SKIP_EXON     = "skip_exon"

@frozen(kw_only=True, auto_attribs=True)   # common/containers.py
class SpliceModel:
    event: SpliceEvent
    index: int          # 0-based, transcript (5'->3') order

@frozen
class SplicedStructure:
    features: tuple[Feature, ...]
    sequence: str
    mapper: Mapper
    cdna_coding_start0: int | None    # None => no start codon under this model
    cds_end0: int | None

On Transcript: spliced_structure (the default model, cached) and spliced_structure_for(model). On TranscriptVariationAllele, two methods — spliced_cds_alleles(model) and spliced_cds_peptide_alleles(model).

The refactor that matters: the edit arithmetic in _full_cds_alleles (footprint, edit_start/edit_end, _edited_boundary, _nucleotide_sequence_up_to_stop) must be written once, taking a SplicedStructure, with the default path passing transcript.spliced_structure. Two copies of that arithmetic is the failure mode to avoid; the regression test for it is that the default structure reproduces today's spliced_seq, transcript_mapper.genomic_spans and cdna_coding_start - 1 exactly.

Both halves are computed under the hypothesis — reference = the modified structure without the variant, alternate = with it — so any difference between them is attributable to the variant alone. A caller wanting hypothesis-vs-normal compares against the existing reference_cds.

docs.title: Constraints discovered while designing
docs.text:
Each of these cost real time to establish; none is obvious from the code:

  • Transcript.cds_start / cds_end do not exist. They are the subject of a pre-existing baseline test failure. Use start_codon_genomic_spans() / stop_codon_genomic_spans(), which do.
  • Derive the intron span from the exon gap, not transcript.introns. introns is an externally-set field (init=False, factory=list) that may be empty or unordered. The gap is always derivable — and it is the strand-sensitive part, so it is where a bug will hide:
  • forward: (exon_k.end + 1, exon_{k+1}.start - 1)
  • reverse (transcript order is genomically descending): (exon_{k+1}.end + 1, exon_k.start - 1)
  • Insert the intron as its own span; do not merge it into a neighbour. Mapper concatenates adjacent spans identically, and inserting needs no strand-specific merge logic.
  • spliced_exons is guaranteed transcript (5'->3') order, index 0 the first exon — documented on the field. The whole design leans on this.
  • Retention and readthrough compose orthogonally. Map cds_end0 through the modified mapper exactly as cdna0 is, and let the existing readthrough field decide whether translation may pass it. A retained intron inside the CDS usually produces a premature stop that _nucleotide_sequence_up_to_stop finds unaided; when it does not, Readthrough.UTR is the already-tested way to ask what happens next. Resist the temptation to make retention imply translate-until-stop — that couples two features that are cleaner apart.
  • Cache per (transcript, model). Bounded by (#introns + #exons) per transcript and shared by every variant hitting the same event, so it amortises well. Add it to spliced_exons's existing invalidates(...) tuple.

docs.title: What to verify when implementing
docs.text:
The gate is unusual and worth stating plainly: because no fact reads a hypothesis, consequence output must be byte-identical. Conformance and verify_requires must stay green, and the suite must match its baseline — compare against the count at the time you start, since the baseline has been in motion.

Beyond that: the default-structure equivalence above (the no-duplication proof); retention growing the sequence by exactly the intron length and skipping shrinking it by exactly the exon length, on both strands; skipping the ATG-bearing exon giving cdna_coding_start0 is None; an out-of-range index returning None rather than raising; and the case that best demonstrates the point — a variant inside a retained intron, which is inert under the normal model (alternate_cds == reference_cds) but has a real effect under retention.

docs.title: Deliberately out of scope
docs.text:
• No inference of which event to model. _nearby_introns and overlap_donor_site/overlap_acceptor_site (facts/position.py) already identify the candidate intron and whether it is disrupted, so auto-triggering later is a small follow-up — but for now the caller names the event.
  • No new SO terms and no second consequence set. Emitting a parallel labelled annotation needs new output plumbing and is a separate decision. A hypothesis is reporting output, not a consequence.
  • No cryptic splice-site modelling, and no combining events — one model, one event.
